answer.rationale: The 18% cost mandate and 14-day renewal window create urgent pressure, but the assembly line's 94% utilization leaves no margin for supply disruption. Memory_c6 shows multi-year commitments unlock volume pricing without narrowing scope—this is directly applicable. Memory_c4 demonstrates that benchmarking against market rates moved the incumbent on both price and payment terms, achieving real margin recovery. Rather than switching (memory_c2's prior success does not guarantee repeatable speed and accuracy under time pressure) or adding second source (complex during crisis), aggressive renegotiation of the incumbent contract offers: (1) preservation of integration stability, (2) direct access to the volume-pricing leverage shown in c6, (3) the demonstrable negotiating wins from c4. The 18% target is severe; a standard renegotiation experiment—bringing market benchmarks and multi-year commitment proposals to the table—tests whether the incumbent will move substantially on price while preserving delivery certainty. If negotiation fails within the 14-day window, deferral to month-to-month (per memory_c5) remains available as fallback, maintaining budget flexibility. This approach minimizes switching risk while directly attacking the cost mandate.
